A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MASC research, with matching authors, methods, and experiments. Their main texts, algorithms, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments measuring model and MASC accuracies under label corruption, including random-initialization controls, optimizer comparisons, and dropout experiments.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds ResNet-18 experiments, alternative-probe comparisons, computational measurements, PCA sensitivity tests, and retraining results.

M1.justification: The PCA-based minimum-angle classifier remains substantively unchanged, but v2 introduces a substantial retraining procedure: select a layer using validation accuracy, relabel the training set with its MASC predictions, and further train the existing network. This extends the method beyond representation probing (Sections 3.4 and 7).

E1.justification: Both versions use MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet for image classification under random label corruption and post-hoc true-label access. ResNet-18, additional probes, and retraining change models or procedures within this coverage, without introducing new datasets or task requirements.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated comparisons against logistic regression, K-nearest neighbors, linear discriminant analysis, quadratic discriminant analysis, and nearest class mean (Section 5 and Appendix C). v1 compares principally against network predictions, early-stopping performance, and random-initialization controls; those existing comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: New retraining experiments reserve 20% of the original test set for layer selection and validation, evaluate on the remaining 80%, and use up to 30 additional epochs with patience 3; a separate experiment uses 10 epochs without early stopping. v2 also adds ResNet-18 layer evaluations, probe-training protocols, and computational-cost and relabeling-error metrics. These additions do not establish changes to the retained experiments' protocols.

E4.justification: v2 replaces the Tiny ImageNet-focused PCA variance sweeps with comparisons of 99%, 75%, 50%, 25%, and one principal component across multiple model-dataset pairs. It adds computational-cost analyses, relabeling error decomposition, and retraining trajectories. Conversely, v1's dropout analyses in Appendix A.11 are removed; the early-stopping and random-initialization controls remain.

E5.justification: Appendix D newly reports five MASC runs using seeds 10, 20, 30, 40, and 50, summarized with means and 95% confidence intervals for PCA sensitivity. These runs use a fixed trained network. The broader practice of averaging three trained instances and displaying their ranges is retained, rather than replaced by five independent training runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds findings on probe accuracy and computational cost, PCA sensitivity, and mixed retraining outcomes. New ResNet-18 results include MASC trailing the model by 0.28 percentage points at 20% corruption (Table 6). The MLP-MNIST random-initialization control curve also changes between v1 Figure 10 and v2 Figure 23. Dropout results disappear, while corresponding retained base-model accuracy rows remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 adds an explicit distributional setup with i.i.d. sampling, separate clean and corrupted-label distributions, and evaluation relative to the clean target distribution. This supplies formal assumptions and definitions for the previously informal setting; no theorem, proof, or new theoretical guarantee is introduced.

C1.justification: The central claim that memorized networks retain decodable generalization is retained. v2 adds contributions concerning alternative probes, computational cost, and improved network performance through MASC-based retraining. It also narrows the corrupted-subspace superiority claim by explicitly acknowledging the ResNet-18/CIFAR-10 exception at 20% corruption.

C2.justification: v2 adds manifold-based motivation, interpretations of differing probe behavior, explanations for retraining successes and failures, and a hypothesis linking stronger generalization to reduced latent memorization. Some new numerical interpretation is inaccurate: Section 7 describes Table 9's -92.46% relative error reduction as 92.46% fewer correct labels, although these are different quantities.

D1.justification: v2 provides a code-repository link and implementation details for the new experiments, including ResNet-18 training settings, logistic regression's optimizer, learning rate, batch size and epochs, KNN's neighbor count and distance, and the retraining pipeline. These materially expand reproducibility information beyond v1's existing model and hardware descriptions.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion and citations for MentorNet, co-teaching, early-learning regularization, and manifold-based motivation, while removing references and discussion concerning Maini's localization work and Feldman's memorization studies. The central positioning against earlier probing and weight-rewinding research remains.

P1.justification: The introduction, contributions, related work, and discussion are substantially rewritten. Algorithms move into the main Methods section, latent memorization moves to Appendix H, and the appendices are reorganized by topic. The terminology consistently distinguishes generalization to true labels from performance on corrupted labels.

P2.justification: v2 adds explanatory schematics for the setting and retraining pipeline, redraws the MASC geometry illustration, expands model-comparison panels, and introduces probe, sensitivity, cost, and retraining displays. Summary tables are expanded and reorganized, early-stopping figures move into the main text, and dropout panels are removed.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence by addressing v1's missing alternative-probe comparisons and extending sensitivity analysis, while testing retraining and documenting failures. Clearer methods and additional implementation information improve assessability and reproducibility. These gains outweigh the loss of preliminary dropout evidence and localized interpretation errors, including Section 7's misreading of Table 9.
